Stanford · Koyejo group · scalable oversight

Watching the watchers:
when do AI judges actually fail?

We tested AI judges with errors we planted ourselves, so the right verdict was never in doubt. Three findings. Judges fail less often than the literature suggests. The answer keys used to measure them fail more often. And the most effective way to help a small judge, showing it a known-correct reference answer, makes judging worse on tasks that have many valid answers. One of our own results was retracted and corrected along the way; the final ones were checked against human-labeled data.

7 judge models, 0.5B to frontier · 6 model families · 5 benchmarks · every planted error verified before use
scroll or press → to advance
The takeaway

Three results, stated up front

1 · A reference helps or hurts, predictably

Show a judge a known-good answer and it gets better at grading tasks with one right answer: 9 percentage points more of its verdicts correct, and the better the reference, the bigger the gain. Show it any reference on a task with many valid answers that it cannot verify by itself, and it gets worse: 7 to 8 points fewer correct verdicts, no matter who wrote the reference (p≤.0005 under a paired test). A controlled synthetic version of both situations reproduced both effects.

2 · A small judge with a reference is nearly frontier-level

Without a reference, a 3B judge catches 17% of hidden errors. With one, 85%, close to frontier level. That boost replicates in all six model families we tried, adding 14 to 60 percentage points of detection. Our reading: comparing against a reference is cheap, even tiny models can do it. Producing the reference is the expensive part.

3 · The measurements themselves were broken

Three textbook-looking "judge failure" effects in our own data turned out to be errors in the benchmarks' grading, 71-83% of the flagged cases once adjudicated. The cleanup also produced a useful tool. When several cheap models unanimously disagree with the official grade, the official grade is the one that is wrong 89% of the time. We validated that rate against a human re-annotation.

What we do not claim. No new judge model, and no formal theory with proofs. The smaller results in this deck (how judges treat typos, which errors they notice, and the order-swap consistency check) are supporting evidence, not headlines.

The problem and the method

Why AI-judging-AI matters, and how we build experiments where the correct verdict is known: we take correct solutions and break them ourselves.

Part 1 · the false discovery

A pattern in our data that looked like a law of judge failure. When we checked the individual cases, most of the "failures" were errors in the benchmark's own answer key. Checking answer keys this way turned out to be cheap and reliable, so we kept it as a tool.

Part 2 · how judges behave

With the labels cleaned up: judging skill rises smoothly with model size, and judges at every size grade the final outcome rather than checking each line of reasoning.

Part 3 · what a reference is worth

Showing the judge a known-correct answer makes small judges far better. We measure the effect, discard one buggy result along the way, and repeat the measurement in six model families.

Part 4 · tasks you cannot check

On tasks with many valid answers, the same reference makes judging worse. Also: a way to measure a judge's reliability with no answer key, by asking the same question twice with the order swapped.

The rules

A practical checklist for anyone building oversight, then the three takeaways again.

Terms used in this deck

Five terms, defined before we use them

AI judge. A model shown a problem and a proposed solution and asked: is this correct? In some experiments it instead sees two responses and picks the better one.
Reference. A known-correct answer shown to the judge next to the solution it is grading. Each experiment states whether the judge got one, and from whom.
Planted error. We take a solution known to be correct and break it ourselves: a subtle changed number, or a wrong value carried consistently through every later step so nothing looks off. Because we made the error, "did the judge catch it?" always has a definite answer.
Answer key. Shorthand for whatever produces the official right/wrong labels: the benchmark's list of correct answers, plus the script that matches a model's answer against it. Either part can be wrong, and when we say "the grading was wrong", we mean this pipeline.
Detection rate and AUC. Detection rate: the share of planted errors a judge flags. AUC: show the judge one right and one wrong solution; how often does it score the wrong one lower? 1.0 means always, 0.5 means it is guessing. AUC does not depend on choosing a pass/fail cutoff, which matters later.
The problem

Why 'AI judging AI' is the question that matters

Modern AI systems produce work no one has time to check: proofs, code, plans, essays. The standard fix is to use another AI as a judge. That only moves the problem, because now someone has to check the judge. This is the field called scalable oversight, and its working assumption is that judges become unreliable as the systems they grade get stronger.

What we set out to do. Measure exactly when and why AI judges fail, using judges of every size, from a 0.5B model that fits on a phone to frontier models, and using errors we planted ourselves, so there is never any doubt about what the right verdict was.

The next slide describes the setup. After that, the results in the order we found them, including the one we got wrong.

The setup

Judges of every size, and errors we control

7judges: 0.5B → frontier
2kinds of planted error
100%of errors verified before use

The judges: the Qwen family at five sizes (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B), plus GPT-5.2 and Claude Opus as the frontier judges. All grade the same solutions under the same instructions.

The errors: we broke known-correct solutions in two ways. A typo changes one number and nothing else. A propagated error changes a value early and carries it through every later step, so the arithmetic all checks out and the text reads smoothly, but the final answer is wrong. A mechanical checker verified every planted error before use: arithmetic consistent, final answer genuinely wrong, no giveaway phrasing. For code, we mutated correct programs and kept only mutants that actually fail the official tests.

The three conditions, which the diagram color-codes. No reference: the judge sees only the problem and the solution it must grade. A correct reference: the judge also sees the benchmark's own known-correct worked solution to the same problem, so it can compare the two. Its own earlier answer: before judging, we ask the same model to solve the problem in a separate, earlier call; whatever it produced, right or wrong, is then pasted in as the reference when it judges. This last condition asks what happens when no trusted reference exists and the judge has to supply its own.
Every result that follows is measured against these verified errors.
Part 1 · the false discovery

A pattern that looked like a law of judge failure

Early on we noticed an interesting pattern: count how many of the small judges a wrong solution fools, and you can predict almost perfectly whether the frontier judge is fooled too. Zero small judges fooled: the frontier fails 1% of the time. All three of the small judges fooled: 94%. It looked like a cheap early-warning system for frontier failures.

Before writing it up, we hand-checked every one of the 55 cases behind the 94%. Most were not judge failures at all. They were correct answers that the benchmark had marked wrong. The judges were right; the answer key was not.

Two other promising effects turned out the same way when we checked their cases. That changed how we ran everything that follows.
Part 1 · a tool from the cleanup

Benchmark answer keys contain measurable error

4-10%of GSM8K grades wrong, depending on model family
89%of consensus flags were real grading bugs
0.66→0.91r² between frontier judge scores and true accuracy, before → after fixing the grading

Three separate "judge failure" effects each turned out to be answer-key errors, not judge errors. That reverses the usual conclusion: a good share of what the literature measures as judge unreliability is answer-key unreliability.

The check is simple. When several cheap open models unanimously disagree with the official grade, the official grade is nearly always what is wrong: usually the answer-matching script misreading a correct answer, occasionally the key itself. We validated this on GSM8K, a standard grade-school math benchmark, against GSM8K-Platinum, its human re-checked version, with no frontier model involved.

Check the answer key before drawing conclusions about the judge.
Part 2 · real behavior

With clean labels, judging skill is a smooth curve

No cliff, no magic threshold where judging "turns on". We also caught ourselves once here: at one choice of pass/fail cutoff on the judge's score, the 7B judge looked identical to the frontier. At a different cutoff the frontier caught 74% of the errors and the 7B caught 10%. The equality was an artifact of where we drew the line, so since then we report threshold-free numbers only.

Judge skill grows smoothly with size.
Part 2 · planted false steps

Judges grade the outcome, not each line

40-50%of explicit false equations go unpenalized
69-85%still receive a passing score at a common cutoff

The pattern to notice: 3B and 14B judges react to how much an error stands out. Frontier judges re-derive the solution and react to whether the error matters. Both styles leave line-level slips unpunished: judges are not reliable step-by-step proofreaders.

Judges of every size grade the final answer; none reliably checks each line.
Part 3 · the mechanism

What a reference is worth, at every judge size

Read the curves one at a time. Red, no reference: small judges catch almost none of the errors, and skill climbs slowly with size. Green, with a correct reference: even the 3B judge now catches 85% of hidden errors. The gap between red and green is what a reference is worth: 68 percentage points of detection at 3B, shrinking to 2 at the frontier, because the frontier can already supply what the reference provides. Purple: the judge generates its own answer first, then judges with it as the reference; it recovers most of the green curve without being handed anything.

What this means. Verification splits into two parts: getting a reference, and comparing against it. Comparing is cheap, tiny models can do it. Getting the reference is the expensive, capability-bound part. The frontier judge gains little from being handed a reference because it can already generate one itself.
Part 3 · the bug

A bug, a retraction, and the corrected result

The first version of the solve-first-then-judge result was wrong. It came out perfect: solving first seemed to recover 100% of the reference benefit at every size. That looked too good, and the giveaway was that its scores were exactly equal to the with-reference condition on all 128 graded items. A code audit found the reason: a bug in our experiment code was silently running the with-reference condition under both labels. We retracted the finding in the log and reran everything with a verified pipeline.

The corrected experiments taught more than the original claim would have:

  • Asking a 7B judge to "solve first, then judge" in a single prompt makes it worse (28% vs 49%). It quietly skips the solving step. Small models fail instructions silently.
  • Forcing the two steps mechanically, generate an answer in one pass, judge with it in the next, is what works: detection of 59% at 1.5B, 60% at 3B, 85% at 7B, 95% at 14B.
  • One result we did not expect: at 1.5B the judge does better with its own imperfect answer as the reference (59%) than with the official textbook solution (21%). A reference in the judge's own style beats a polished one it finds foreign.
Six of our own preliminary results failed our own checks during this project. This bug was the most instructive.
Part 3 · does it generalize?

The reference boost replicates in six families and on human-labeled data

The effect is not specific to Qwen models, and not specific to our planted errors.
Part 4 · the real frontier

The hard part: tasks where you cannot check the answer

Everything so far involved tasks that can be checked: math has answer keys, code has tests. Oversight is hardest on tasks without either: open-ended writing, judgment calls, questions with many valid answers. So the question became: does giving the judge a reference, the most effective intervention so far, still help there?

The experiment. RewardBench-2 is a benchmark of response pairs, one better and one worse, across task types from fully checkable (math) to many-valid-answers (open questions). Note that the judge's task changes here: it now picks the better of two responses. We ran every judge size over 460 prompts. Each pair was judged twice, in both orders: if the verdict changes when the two responses swap places, it depended on presentation order, not content. Three conditions: no reference, the judge's own answer as reference, and, as a control, another model's answer as reference.
Part 4 · order-swap consistency

Ask twice, swapped: a reliability check that needs no answer key

Two things worth noticing. First, this measurement needs no ground truth: you just ask the same question twice with the order swapped. Second, the one line that never improves: judging precise instruction compliance ("did the response really obey every stated constraint?") stays near chance at every size we tested. This matches Part 2: checking every stated constraint is line-by-line work, and judges of every size skip it.

Instruction-compliance judging fails not because the task is ambiguous but because it requires line-by-line checking, which judges skip.
Part 4 · the finding

On many-valid-answer tasks, references make judging worse

The control condition answers why. If the harm came from the judge favoring its own writing, references written by other models would be harmless. They are not: they hurt by the same amount. What actually happens: on a question with many valid answers, any single reference anchors the judge to one of them, and it starts punishing other, perfectly valid answers for being different.

We then rebuilt the situation synthetically: tasks with several valid answers where checking validity is trivial. There the harm disappears for every judge 3B and up. So the rule needs both conditions at once: many valid answers, and verification too hard for the judge to do itself.

One right answer: give the judge a reference. Many valid answers the judge cannot verify: do not.
What it adds up to

Practical rules for anyone building oversight today

Measurement

  • Audit the grading first, both the script and the key. When several cheap models unanimously disagree with the official grade, the grade is wrong 89% of the time, with no extra human labeling needed.
  • Never trust one threshold. A single cutoff produced a spurious "7B equals frontier" result in our own data. Report threshold-free numbers.
  • Judge each pair twice, with the order swapped. The order-flip rate is a reliability check that needs no ground truth.

Judges are not proofreaders

  • Explicit false steps pass 40-85% of the time. Judges grade outcomes and coherence, not lines. Do not use raw judge scores as step-level process rewards.

The reference rule

  1. One right answer? Give the judge a reference; quality matters, and even a small judge becomes reliable. No trusted reference available? Have the judge generate one in a separate, forced generation step. Do not just tell it to solve first inside one prompt; small judges skip the instruction silently.
  2. Many valid answers? Withhold references entirely. Any reference, from any source, anchors the judge against valid alternatives: 7 to 8 points worse, p≤.0005.
  3. Precise constraint checking? No judge we tested does it reliably. Use programmatic checkers.
The takeaway, once more

If you remember three things

  • References are the main design choice. They make small judges nearly frontier-level on single-answer tasks, and they hurt on many-valid-answer tasks the judge cannot verify itself. Which way it goes depends on two known conditions: how many valid answers exist, and whether the judge can verify them.
  • Most of the cost of oversight is producing references. Comparing against one is easy, even for small models. Budget should go into producing good references before it goes into bigger judges.
  • Check the answer key before drawing conclusions about the judge. Most of our apparent judge failures were grading failures, and unanimous disagreement from a handful of cheap models finds those at 89% precision.

APPENDIX

What was checked, which of our own results we withdrew, and the questions we left open.

Appendix · the record

What was checked, and how

15findings
6preliminary results withdrawn after failing our own checks
1public retraction with correction
4independent critic passes

Every headline number was re-derived from the raw files with fresh code. Planted code errors were re-executed against the official test suites. The answer-key findings rest on two frontier model families agreeing on all 55 disputed cases we re-checked, plus the external check against a human re-annotation. We also read the closest prior paper carefully to confirm the reference-harm result is new: that paper tests only single-answer tasks, scores one response at a time, and has no control conditions like ours.

Appendix · open questions

What we did not settle

  • Can a model verify only what it could itself generate? That hypothesis is common in the field. The correlation we saw item by item is weak; a proper answer needs more data.
  • Human spot-audits of our model-based adjudications. Two frontier families agreeing is strong but is not a human check.
  • Agent-trajectory oversight. Existing benchmarks cover safety labels; planting verified flaws inside agent trajectories, the analogue of what we did for math and code, is future work.
  • Frontier arms on the hard-to-verify experiments. The sign-flip result is established up to 14B; the frontier row of that table is incomplete.
All data, instruments, and scripts are in the repo; the log records every dead end as well as every result.
